content: Stress is the body's response to any demand or challenge, known scientifically as a stressor. In men, stress triggers complex physiological mechanisms primarily governed by the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and sympathetic nervous system. These systems release hormones such as cortisol and adrenaline, resulting in 'fight-or-flight' responses. Stress can be acute or chronic; chronic stress may negatively impact men's health by increasing risks for cardiovascular disease, mental health disorders such as anxiety and depression, and impairing immune function. The experience and effects of stress in men can differ from women due to hormonal and psychosocial differences, although there's substantial individual variability. Practically, managing stress involves lifestyle changes (exercise, diet, sleep), relaxation techniques (meditation, deep breathing), and sometimes professional support. Synonyms and related terms include psychophysiological stress, tension, and strain. Limitations in current knowledge include variability in biomarkers and subjective experiences, as well as challenges in isolating stress effects from other health determinants. Safety considerations emphasize avoiding harmful coping strategies like substance use. Understanding stress in men supports prevention and early intervention, improving overall quality of life and reducing health risks.

chunk_title: Physiology of Stress in Men: The HPA Axis and Sympathetic Nervous System
content: The stress response in men involves activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and the sympathetic nervous system (SNS). Stressors stimulate hypothalamic release of corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH), leading to pituitary secretion of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), which triggers adrenal cortisol release. Cortisol facilitates energy mobilization and modulates immune and cardiovascular responses. Concurrently, the SNS releases adrenaline, preparing muscles for 'fight-or-flight.' Differences in male sex hormones like testosterone may modulate these responses.
